title: The Illusion of Significance: Rethinking the p-value Through A/B Testing
text:
In statistics textbooks, the p-value seems to offer a clear verdict: if \(p < 0.05\), the result is significant, and the experiment is a success. However, when I stepped into the role of a data science intern at an internet company, reality presented a very different picture. During my time running A/B tests, I frequently encountered experiments with incredibly small p-values that yielded zero actual business benefit. Conversely, genuinely effective features sometimes failed to show significance due to high variance.
This paradox reveals the most counterintuitive aspect of the p-value: it is not the probability you think it is. The most common misconception is equating the p-value with the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or \(P(H_0 \mid \text{Data})\). We desperately want to know: “Given this data, what is the probability that my experiment actually worked?” But the p-value answers a completely reversed question: \(P(\text{Data} \mid H_0)\), which asks, “Assuming my experiment had absolutely no effect, what is the probability of observing a difference this large purely by chance?” This is a transposed conditional probability:
\[P(\text{Data} \mid H_0) \neq P(H_0 \mid \text{Data})\]
Think of a courtroom: the p-value is not the probability that the defendant is innocent; it is the probability of finding the current evidence if the defendant were completely innocent. This logical inversion is why the p-value initially feels so unintuitive.



The geometric meaning of the p-value: the probability of observing a result as extreme as the current one, assuming the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is true.

title: The Illusion of Significance: Rethinking the p-value Through A/B Testing
text:
The Illusion of Significance
Understanding this helped me navigate the illusions I faced during my internship. When we simultaneously tracked dozens of metrics, even if the product changed nothing, random fluctuations meant roughly 5% of these metrics would naturally show a \(p < 0.05\). This is the problem of multiple testing. To filter out these false positives, we cannot blindly trust a single p-value. For a strict control of the family-wise error rate, we use the Bonferroni correction:
\[\alpha_{\text{Bonferroni}} = \frac{\alpha}{m}\]
where \(m\) is the number of hypotheses tested. Alternatively, to control the false discovery rate, we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure:
\[\text{Reject } H_{(i)} \text{ if } p_{(i)} \leq \frac{i}{m} \alpha\]



Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure


Furthermore, we used the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) to check if our traffic split was truly uniform. If the control and experimental groups were inherently different before the test even began, the post-experiment p-value would be a misleading illusion:
\[\text{SMD} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\text{treatment}} - \bar{X}_{\text{control}}}{\sqrt{\frac{s_{\text{treatment}}^2 + s_{\text{control}}^2}{2}}}\]

title: The Illusion of Significance: Rethinking the p-value Through A/B Testing
text:
The Missing Significance
On the other hand, p-values can also fail to detect the truth. Often, a beneficial feature would be launched, but due to insufficient sample size or inherently noisy user behavior, the p-value would fail to reach significance. To address this, we applied CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data). It uses pre-experiment covariates to reduce variance, allowing a true effect that was previously drowned out by noise to finally emerge:
\[Y_{\text{cuped}} = Y - \theta (X - \bar{X})\]
where the optimal \(\theta\) is derived as:
\[\theta = \frac{\text{Cov}(Y, X)}{\text{Var}(X)}\]



CUPED Explained

title: The Illusion of Significance: Rethinking the p-value Through A/B Testing
text:
Historical Context
Historically, this awkward position of the p-value is nothing new. In 1925, statistician Ronald Fisher casually suggested using a 5% threshold for agricultural experiments. He likely never anticipated that this arbitrary cutoff would become an almost sacred dogma in both academia and industry for nearly a century.
Today, the American Statistical Association explicitly warns that “a p-value does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.” My internship experience is a perfect testament to this. The p-value is merely a measure of “surprise.” It does not represent business value, nor can it be interpreted in isolation from experimental design, traffic quality, or data variance. Understanding the counterintuitive nature of the p-value is not about rejecting it, but about approaching data—and business intuition—with a healthy dose of humility.

title: The Illusion of Significance: Rethinking the p-value Through A/B Testing

title: SEPTA Metro and Trolley: A Guide for a New Penn Student
text:
For a new student at the University of Pennsylvania (Penn), public transportation is an important part of getting around Philadelphia. Students may need to travel to different neighborhoods, shopping areas, restaurants, or other parts of the city. SEPTA provides several types of public transportation, including Metro and trolley services. However, for someone who is new to Philadelphia, it can be difficult to understand which lines and stations are most convenient from the Penn campus.
In this project, I used web scraping to collect SEPTA transportation information and answer a practical question: Which SEPTA Metro and Trolley lines are most accessible to a new Penn student?
The data came from the OpenDataPhilly website, specifically the SEPTA “Routes, Stops, and Locations” dataset. I used the rvest package in R to scrape the webpage and identify the available CSV data files. I then used the station and stop datasets to examine SEPTA Metro and trolley routes. The datasets contain information such as route names, station or stop names, and geographic coordinates.
For the Metro data, I used the High Speed Stations dataset. It contains information for three main routes in the dataset: B, L, and M. For the trolley data, I used the Trolley Stations dataset, which contains trolley stop names, route abbreviations, and latitude and longitude coordinates.
After collecting the data, I cleaned the datasets and combined the Metro and trolley information. I used an approximate location for the Penn campus as the reference point. Then, I calculated the approximate straight-line distance between Penn and each SEPTA station or trolley stop. This allowed me to compare the geographic accessibility of different SEPTA lines.

title: SEPTA Metro and Trolley: A Guide for a New Penn Student
text:
2 Results
The first chart shows the nearest SEPTA Metro or trolley stop for each route. The trolley stops around 36th Street and 33rd Street are very close to Penn. The L Line also has a station at 34th Street, which is approximately 0.27 miles from the reference point on the Penn campus. These locations are particularly close compared with some other SEPTA routes.






Figure 1: Nearest SEPTA Metro or Trolley Stop to Penn



The B Line has a nearby station at Walnut–Locust, although it is farther from Penn than the L Line and the trolley stops. The M Line and D routes have their closest stops several miles away from Penn. Therefore, based only on geographic distance, these routes are less directly accessible from the Penn campus.
The second chart shows the number of SEPTA stops within one mile of Penn. The results show that several trolley routes and the L Line have stops within this distance. This provides another way to understand which routes may be convenient for a student who wants to walk to a SEPTA stop.






Figure 2: SEPTA Stops Within One Mile of Penn



The third chart provides another visualization of the SEPTA transportation data collected for this project.






Figure 3: SEPTA Metro and Trolley Data

title: SEPTA Metro and Trolley: A Guide for a New Penn Student
text:
3 Actionable Insight
For a new Penn student, the results suggest that the trolley routes around 33rd and 36th Streets and the L Line at 34th Street are geographically close to campus. These routes may therefore be useful starting points when learning how to use SEPTA.
The results also show why understanding the location of stops is useful. A student does not necessarily need to know every SEPTA route immediately. Instead, they can first learn the stations and trolley stops that are closest to campus and then use those locations as starting points for trips around Philadelphia.
However, distance alone does not determine whether a route is convenient. Travel time, destination, service frequency, transfers, and current service conditions can also affect the usefulness of a route. Therefore, this analysis should be viewed as a simple geographic comparison rather than a complete evaluation of SEPTA service.

title: SEPTA Metro and Trolley: A Guide for a New Penn Student
text:
4 Limitations
There are several limitations to this analysis. First, the distance calculation is an approximate straight-line distance rather than actual walking distance. A station that is geographically close may require a longer walking route because of streets, buildings, or other obstacles.
Second, some SEPTA stops are shared by multiple trolley routes. The dataset may represent these routes together, so the route names in the charts can sometimes appear as combinations such as T1, T2, T3, T4, and T5.
Finally, the datasets used in this project are GIS datasets rather than real-time service information. SEPTA schedules and service conditions can change, so students should check current SEPTA information before planning a specific trip.

title: SEPTA Metro and Trolley: A Guide for a New Penn Student
text:
5 Conclusion
This project demonstrates how web scraping can be used to answer a practical transportation question. By scraping SEPTA information from OpenDataPhilly and analyzing station locations in R, I was able to compare the geographic accessibility of different Metro and trolley routes from the Penn campus. The analysis shows that several trolley stops and the L Line are located relatively close to Penn, providing useful starting points for a new student learning to navigate Philadelphia using SEPTA.

title: How Does Labor Force Participation Vary Across Age, Gender, and Education?
text: Labor force participation is an important indicator of how different groups engage with the U.S. labor market. In this post, I use IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) microdata to examine how labor force participation varies across age, gender, and educational attainment. The analysis uses monthly CPS observations from 2020 through 2025 and focuses on individuals age 16 and older. I use the CPS person-level final weight (WTFINL) when calculating participation rates so that the results reflect the U.S. population rather than simply the raw survey sample.

title: How Does Labor Force Participation Vary Across Age, Gender, and Education?
text:
Labor Force Participation Across Age
The first visualization shows a clear life-cycle pattern in labor force participation.






Figure 1: Labor Force Participation Rate by Age Group, U.S., 2020–2025.



The weighted participation rate is 55.7% among individuals ages 16–24, but it rises sharply to 83.0% among those ages 25–34 and 83.5% among those ages 35–44. Participation remains relatively high among people ages 45–54 at 81.7%, before declining to 65.8% for ages 55–64. Among people age 65 and older, the rate falls to only 19.7%. This pattern suggests substantial differences in labor-force attachment across stages of the life cycle. Younger people may still be completing their education, while older individuals are more likely to have left the labor force.

title: How Does Labor Force Participation Vary Across Age, Gender, and Education?
section: Gender Differences Across the Life Cycle
text:
Gender Differences Across the Life Cycle
The second visualization adds gender to the analysis.






Figure 2: Labor Force Participation Rate by Age and Gender, U.S., 2020–2025.



The age pattern differs noticeably between men and women. Among 16–24-year-olds, participation is relatively similar: 56.5% for men and 54.9% for women. However, the difference becomes larger among prime-age adults. For example, among people ages 35–44, participation is 90.1% for men compared with 76.9% for women, a difference of 13.2 percentage points. The gap remains among older workers: participation among those age 65 and older is 24.0% for men and 16.1% for women.

title: How Does Labor Force Participation Vary Across Age, Gender, and Education?
text:
Education and Labor Force Participation
The third visualization combines age and educational attainment.






Figure 3: Labor Force Participation Rate by Age and Education, U.S., 2020–2025.



The heatmap shows substantial differences across education groups, particularly among prime-age adults. For example, among individuals ages 35–44, participation ranges from 69.1% for those with less than a high school education to 89.1% for those with a bachelor’s degree or higher. A similar educational gradient appears among people ages 45–54 and 55–64. However, the pattern is less straightforward among younger individuals. Among 16–24-year-olds, for example, participation is 61.5% for those with some college or an associate degree, compared with 68.2% for those with a high school diploma. This may partly reflect the fact that many young adults are still enrolled in education.

title: How Does Labor Force Participation Vary Across Age, Gender, and Education?
text:
Conclusion
Overall, the three visualizations show that labor force participation varies substantially across the life cycle and that gender and educational attainment are associated with different participation patterns. The strongest differences appear among prime-age and older adults. These results are descriptive rather than causal, but they illustrate how CPS microdata can be used to explore important patterns in the U.S. labor market.

title: How Does Labor Force Participation Vary Across Age, Gender, and Education?
text:
